analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to offer free online tax preparation, filing software, and simple return preparation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2016 with 9 Senate supporters, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the IRS to build and run, free of charge, online tax preparation and filing software for all taxpayers. It would also have let taxpayers download the wage, interest, and dividend information the government already receives from employers and banks, and would have let people with simple finances have the IRS prepare and file their return for them. It barred the Treasury Department from signing any agreement that restricts the government's right to offer these services, aimed at the existing arrangement with commercial tax-filing companies.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 150 million people who file individual income tax returns each year, especially the tens of millions with simple wage-based finances who currently pay for commercial filing software or paid preparers. Taxpayers would no longer need to buy software or pay preparation fees just to file a return the government already has the data for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, especially those with simple returns

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to establish and operate free online tax preparation and filing software, available to all taxpayers by January 31, 2018 [S2][S3].

Requires the IRS to create a program letting taxpayers download the third-party wage, interest, and dividend information the government already receives, in printable and computer-readable form, within 15 days of the IRS receiving it [S2][S3].

Creates a program under which individuals with simplified tax situations can elect to have the IRS prepare their return at no fee, with eligibility to be expanded at the Secretary's discretion after 2017 to married filers, parents claiming the child tax credit, and others [S2][S3].

Prohibits the Treasury Secretary from entering into any agreement that restricts the government's legal right to provide tax return preparation, software, or filing services, and prohibits any fee on taxpayers using the new programs [S2][S3].
Speeds up filing deadlines for employer wage reports and other information returns to January 31, so the IRS has the data in time to prefill returns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies, whose paid filing products would face direct free competition from the government. Taxpayers collectively would fund building and running the new IRS systems through annual appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The free IRS-prepared-return program would cover only a narrow group at first — unmarried filers taking the standard deduction with only wage, interest, or dividend income — so many filers would still need software or a preparer for complex returns [S3].
Building and securing new IRS filing systems would require federal appropriations of unspecified size for fiscal years 2017 through 2021, and the bill relies on Congress actually funding it [S3].

Putting the government in the role of both preparer and enforcer of taxes raised security and accuracy concerns; the bill addresses this by requiring identity verification and stating taxpayers remain responsible for their returns' accuracy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary filers the direct benefit is concrete: filing that is free, and for simple situations largely automatic, because the government already holds the underlying data. The main costs fall on an industry, not on filers, though taxpayers would fund the new systems and early eligibility for government-prepared returns would be narrow.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on April 13, 2016, joined by eight cosponsors — seven Democrats and one Independent [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
That referral was the last action ever recorded; the Finance Committee held no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].

The bill would also have barred Treasury from signing agreements restricting government tax filing services, a challenge to the private-industry Free File arrangement, and would have banned fees on taxpayers using the new IRS programs [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial tax preparation and software companies kept their market, since a free government alternative never advanced. Tens of millions of filers kept paying for commercial filing software and paid preparation. Taxpayers, filing individuals who would have used the service, are worse off because the bill never advanced; the tax preparation software industry is better off because its market was not opened to free government competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax prep software companies and paid preparers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Filing Simplification Act of 2016 on April 13, 2016

for.name: 8 Senate cosponsors (7 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Original cosponsors including Sens. Shaheen, Baldwin, Sanders, Franken, Udall, Whitehouse, Markey, and Leahy

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Committee on Finance, 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Finance Committee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it sat without action until the Congress ended

against.name: Tax preparation and tax software industry (Intuit, H&R Block and allied preparers)
against.role: Commercial providers of paid tax preparation and filing software
against.what_they_did: Opposed government free-filing proposals and lobbied to preserve the private Free File arrangement that the bill would have overridden

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters were Democrats or the chamber's Independent (Sanders); the bill sat in a Finance Committee led by a Republican chair and never received a hearing or vote, and no Republican supported it on the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Tax preparation and filing software companies (Intuit/TurboTax, H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt)
industries.note: The bill would have forced these companies to compete with free IRS filing software and a free IRS-prepared-return option, cutting into fees Americans pay to file. Their interest in keeping paid filing as the default channel ran directly against taxpayers who wanted a free government alternative [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Paid tax preparers and refund-advance lenders
industries.note: Free IRS preparation for simple returns and faster availability of wage data would reduce demand for paid preparation and refund products sold to working filers [S3].
The bill would have charged the IRS with building and running new free filing systems at public expense, expanding its direct service role to taxpayers while requiring appropriations to do it [S3].
